_convention._1_source_of_truth: en.json is THE source of truth for key names. fr.json mirrors this structure exactly — same keys, same nesting, same order. Never add a key to fr.json that does not exist here.
_convention._2_naming: Namespaced dot-paths, lowerCamelCase leaf names: <area>.<surface>.<element>. Examples: auth.login.title, auth.register.emailLabel, nav.dashboard, common.cancel, errors.invalidEmail.
_convention._3_areas: common.* = reused across two or more surfaces (buttons, field labels, generic words). auth.* = login / register / forgot-password. nav.* = navbar + account menu. errors.* = validation and failure messages. Add a new top-level area per surface group as later rounds land (dashboard.*, cv.*, interview.*).
_convention._4_no_duplicates: A string used on two surfaces lives in common.* and is referenced from both. Do NOT copy the same English text under two page keys — that is how translations drift apart.
_convention._5_fallback: Missing or empty keys fall back to English (fallbackLng: 'en', returnEmptyString: false). An untranslated surface renders English, never a blank or a raw key path — which is what lets translation ship surface by surface.
_convention._6_interpolation: Use named placeholders: "{{year}}", "{{label}}". escapeValue is false because React escapes already. NOTE: "count" is reserved by i18next for pluralization — a key using {{count}} MUST be declared as <key>_one / <key>_other in every locale (see nav.account.creditsLeft). Use a different placeholder name, e.g. {{n}}, when you do not want plural handling.
_convention._7_untranslated: Legal and billing copy (Terms of Service, Privacy Policy bodies) is deliberately NOT translated — it needs a qualified reviewer, not a best guess. See auth.register.legal.*.

target_job.thesis: Set the target and everything aims at it — tailoring is what beats the ATS.

points.0: The ATS matches the job's exact keywords — a set target lets ARIA weave them in.

heading.thesis: The first thing scanned — keep it clean, professional, and ATS-safe.

points.0: Name (biggest), one phone, a professional email (first.last@ — not a nickname).
points.1: City + country is enough — skip your full street address.
points.2: Add your LinkedIn (90%+ of recruiters check it) + a portfolio/GitHub if you have one.
points.3: Plain text — no photo or icon labels; they confuse the ATS.

heading.source: How recruiters + ATS read your header

history.thesis: Recruiters read this hardest — and reward achievements, not duties.

points.0: Lead with what you achieved, not what you were "responsible for."
points.1: Shape each line: did [action] → [result] → [a number] (the XYZ formula).
points.2: Quantify — %, time, money, scale. No number? Use scale ("across 40+ tickets a day").
points.3: 3–5 lines per role, strongest first, aimed at the job you want.

history.after: Cut response time ~30% by streamlining triage across 40+ daily tickets.
history.source: How recruiters & ATS actually read CVs

projects.thesis: A project says "I chose to build this" — so the why, your role & the tech matter most.

points.0: Say what it does and the problem it solves.
points.1: Make your part clear — what you built vs. the team.
points.2: Name the tech & tools — projects are where your skills show.
points.3: Show the outcome (users, a grade, it shipped) + add a link.
points.4: Course, personal, or work project? Each is framed a little differently.

projects.example: Built a ride-matching app in React & Node for my capstone — cut match time to <2s, demoed to 200+ students.

education.thesis: As a student, this does heavy lifting — give it detail, near the top.

points.1: Add your GPA if it's 3.5+ and recent; leave it off otherwise.
points.2: Little work experience? List 2–4 relevant courses that match the job.
points.3: Include honors / Dean's List — they show consistency.

education.example: BSc Computer Science, University of Lagos — 2025 · GPA 3.7 · Dean's List · Relevant: Data Structures, Databases
education.source: How new-grad education sections are read

skills.thesis: Skills get you past the robot — match the job's words exactly, don't pad.

points.0: About 70% hard skills (tools, tech), 30% soft — roughly 8–15 hard + 3–5 soft.
points.1: Use the job's exact words: it says "Salesforce" → don't write "CRM software" (ATS won't match).
points.2: List only what you've actually used — no buzzword padding.
points.3: Prove soft skills in your experience bullets, not as adjectives here.

skills.example: Python · React · SQL · AWS · Figma — the tools the job actually named.
skills.source: How ATS keyword-matching + recruiters read skills

summary.thesis: A tight 2–4 line pitch: who you are, your best skills, one real win.

points.0: 2–4 sentences (~50–60 words) — a snapshot, not a story.
points.1: Lead with your strongest relevant skills + a quantified achievement.
points.2: Tailor it — mirror the target job's keywords. Third person, no "I".
points.3: Little experience? Lead with education + transferable skills.

finalize.thesis: A CV is ready when it's tailored, tight, and clean.

points.0: Every line tailored to this job — cut anything generic.
points.1: Achievements quantified where you can; no "responsible for."
points.2: One page if you can; consistent formatting; proofread twice.
points.3: Save as PDF so it looks the same everywhere.

bodyLanguage.heading: Walk in with presence
bodyLanguage.subtitle: How you show up speaks before you do. A few habits that read as confident:

0.title: The first 7 seconds
0.body: Impressions form almost instantly. Walk in with shoulders back, a warm smile, and unhurried, purposeful steps.

1.title: Posture
1.body: Sit tall with an open chest; lean in slightly when listening. Don’t shrink, slouch, or fold your arms.

2.title: Eye contact
2.body: Hold it ~4–5 seconds at a time — connection, not a stare. On video, look into the camera, not your own face.

3.title: Handshake & hands
3.body: If offered, a firm (not crushing) grip with a smile. Rest your hands calmly and let them gesture naturally.

4.title: Power pose
4.body: Two minutes standing tall, hands on hips, before you go in. It genuinely lifts confidence and lowers stress.

5.title: Voice & pace
5.body: Slow down. A breath before you answer beats filler words, and a calm, warm tone reads as confident.

running.defaultWeakness:
A strong weakness answer is personal, honest, and growth-oriented. Follow these principles:

1. **State a genuine weakness**: Choose a real growth area or technical skill you previously lacked. Avoid cliches like 'I'm a perfectionist'.
2. **Explain the steps you've taken**: Detail the concrete actions you've executed to improve (e.g., enrolling in a course, reading, seeking feedback).
3. **Show positive progress**: Conclude by demonstrating how you apply your learning to turn this gap into a strength.
running.defaultStar:
Structure your answer using the STAR framework:

• **Situation**: Outline the context or problem you faced.
• **Task**: Explain the goal or responsibility you had.
• **Action**: Describe the specific actions you took (focus on *your* contributions).
• **Result**: Share the quantitative outcomes, lessons learned, or improvements.

sources.1: Volunteering, NYSC, or a church/community role
sources.2: Student societies, class rep, a club you helped run
sources.3: Side hustles, freelance work, anything you built or sold
sources.4: Internships, industrial training, or holiday work
sources.5: Something you taught yourself and then actually used

grad.closer: Pick the example with the most detail you can remember — what the situation was, what YOU did, and how it turned out.

experienced.headline: Bring specifics, not job descriptions
experienced.body: You have the material. What separates a strong answer from a flat one is detail:

sources.0: A situation you personally owned, not what your team generally did
sources.1: The decision you made and what you traded off
sources.2: Numbers where you have them — size, time, money, volume, percentage
sources.3: What actually happened afterwards, including when it went badly
sources.4: Work outside your job title: side projects, mentoring, things you fixed

experienced.closer: If you cannot remember an exact number, say the scale honestly rather than inventing one — a made-up figure is the fastest way to lose a real interview.

changer.headline: Evidence from your old field still counts

sources.0: Transferable work from your previous field — the skill, not the job title
sources.1: Projects, courses or certifications from the switch itself
sources.2: Anything you have built, freelanced or volunteered in the new field

listening.title: What Interviewers Are Actually Listening For
listening.p1: Behind every question, an interviewer is listening for one thing: signal. Evidence that you can do the job. Proof that you've thought about this role specifically. A sense that you'd be good to have on the team.
listening.p2: Vague, generic, or rehearsed-sounding answers are noise — they could come from any candidate for any job. The candidates who stand out aren't the smoothest talkers; they're the ones who give specific, evidenced answers that clearly map to what the role needs.
listening.p3: Everything below — the STAR method, the question playbook, and how we score you — is really about one goal: turning what you've genuinely done into clear, convincing signal.

star.title: The STAR Method — the Backbone of Strong Answers
star.subcopy: The single most reliable way to structure a behavioural answer. Four beats that turn a vague memory into a story that lands.
star.situationBody: Set the scene in one or two sentences. Just enough context for the story to make sense — don't over-explain.
star.taskBody: What were you responsible for? What was the goal or the problem you had to solve?
star.actionBody: What did YOU personally do? This is the heart of it — "we" hides your contribution, "I" reveals it.
star.resultBody: How did it end? Quantify wherever you honestly can — "cut processing time 30%" beats "it went well."
star.sampleQuestion: "Tell me about a time you solved a difficult problem."
star.weakBody: "We had a lot of issues with our system being slow, so I worked with the team and we fixed it. Everyone was happy with the result and it was a good experience."
star.weakNote: No specifics, no "I", no measurable outcome. It could be anyone, on any project.
star.starBody: "Our checkout page was timing out for about 1 in 5 users <s1>(Situation)</s1>. I owned fixing it before the holiday rush <s2>(Task)</s2>. I profiled the requests, found an un-indexed database query, added the index and cached the slowest call <s3>(Action)</s3>. Load time dropped from 4.2s to 0.8s and checkout completion rose 12% that month <s4>(Result)</s4>."
star.starNote: Specific, owned, measurable. This is the answer that earns the score.

questionTypes.title: The Six Question Types — and How to Handle Each
questionTypes.subcopy: Almost every interview question is a variation of these. Know the move for each and nothing catches you off guard.
questionTypes.q1Approach: A tight 60–90s narrative: present (what you do now) → past (the experience that got you here) → why-here (why this role, this company). Not your life story — a trailer for the rest of the interview.
questionTypes.q2Approach: Pure STAR territory. Reach for a real, specific story with a concrete outcome. The interviewer is testing whether your example holds up under follow-up questions — so pick ones you actually lived.
questionTypes.q3Approach: They care about your reasoning more than the "right" answer. Think out loud, name the trade-offs, explain why you'd choose one path over another. Show the decisions, not just the conclusion.
questionTypes.q4Approach: This is where research shows. Reference something specific about the team, product, or mission — and connect it to what you genuinely want next. Generic flattery reads as "I'll take any job."
questionTypes.q5Approach: Name a real one and what you're actively doing about it. Skip the humble-brags ("I work too hard") — they're transparent. Self-awareness plus a plan is the signal they want.
questionTypes.q6Approach: Never say "no." Have 2–3 thoughtful questions ready about the team, the challenges of the role, or how success is measured. It's your last chance to show genuine interest.

checklist.title: Before & During — the Practical Checklist
checklist.before1: Research the company and the role — read the job description twice and find something specific about the team or product.
checklist.before2: Know your own CV cold. Every line is fair game for a follow-up.
checklist.before3: Prepare 5–6 STAR stories mapped to the competencies the role likely tests.
checklist.before4: Rehearse out loud — not in your head. Saying it is a different skill from thinking it.
checklist.before5: Prepare your 2–3 questions for them in advance.
checklist.during1: Answer the question that was actually asked — don't pivot to a rehearsed speech.
checklist.during2: Be specific and quantify whenever you honestly can.
checklist.during3: Stay honest. Never claim what you can't back up — it unravels under follow-ups.
checklist.during4: Keep answers to roughly 60–90 seconds, then stop and let them dig in.
checklist.during5: Ask a clarifying question if you need one — it's a strength, not a weakness.
checklist.deliveryBody: In a real, in-person interview, delivery matters too — eye contact (or camera contact on video), steady pacing, structure over rambling, staying calm under pressure. Our score reads a transcript, so it judges your content only — but in the room, how you say it counts. Practise both.
checklist.mistake1: Vague, generic answers that could fit any job
checklist.mistake2: Going off-topic or rambling past the point
checklist.mistake5: Having no questions at the end
checklist.mistake6: Claiming skills or experience not on your CV

rounds.title: Real Interviews Come in Rounds
rounds.subcopy: Most hiring processes aren't one conversation — they're a sequence of rounds, each with a different person looking for something different.
rounds.r1Body: First contact. They're checking motivation, basic fit, and whether your story holds together — "why this role, why now?"
rounds.r2Body: A deep dive with someone who does your job. Here it's all about depth, reasoning, and real examples of your work.
rounds.r3Body: The person who'll lead you. They weigh role fit, how you'd work with the team, and whether they want you on it.
rounds.closer: That's exactly why ApplyRight lets you pick your interviewer and run each round in any order — it mirrors a real hiring loop, so you practise the whole journey, not just one chat.

rubric.title: How ApplyRight Scores Your Mock Interview
rubric.subcopy: No black box. After every interview we read your transcript and rate it across seven dimensions — the same things real interviewers look for. Here's exactly how it works.
rubric.d1Body: Do your answers speak to what this specific job actually needs — or could they apply to any job anywhere?
rubric.d2Body: Real examples, names, numbers, outcomes. Concrete beats abstract every single time.
rubric.d3Body: Are your stories organised — situation, task, action, result — or do they wander and trail off?
rubric.d4Body: Clear, focused answers that get to the point. Rambling buries your best material.
rubric.d5Body: Genuine understanding of the work, not surface-level buzzwords — and a fit for the seniority of the role.
rubric.d6Body: Do you show real interest in this role and company, or could this be a script for anyone?
rubric.d7Body: Your spoken answers should match your CV. Claims it can't back up are flagged as overreach.
rubric.bandNeedsWorkBody: Answers are too vague or generic to show you're ready yet.
rubric.bandAlmostBody: Solid, evidenced answers that are nearly there.
rubric.fp1Bold: It judges content, not your voice.
rubric.fp1Body: The score reads a transcript — your tone, accent, and audio quality never affect it. Only what you said.
rubric.fp2Body: Claims your CV can't support are flagged as overreach under "Consistency with CV" and count against you.
rubric.fp3Body: If you barely answer (under ~40 characters total), you score 0. Give real, complete answers out loud — about 60–90 seconds each.
rubric.fp4Body: Per-dimension scores plus Strengths, Gaps to close, and Practice next — viewable per interviewer in the Reviews tab.

faq.title: Questions, Answered
faq.q1A: It's honest, not cruel. It rewards specific, evidenced, role-relevant answers and is candid about vague or generic ones — so the feedback actually helps you improve. Solid, well-evidenced answers comfortably clear the "almost" band.
faq.q2Q: Does my accent affect my score?
faq.q2A: No. The score reads a transcript of what you said — it judges content only. Your accent, tone, pace, and audio quality have zero effect on it.
faq.q3Q: How many minutes do I need?
faq.q3A: You get a free 5-minute taste to try it, no card needed. Each round is short, so that's enough to complete a full interview and get scored. Longer practice uses metered live-interview minutes.
faq.q4A: Yes. Run an interviewer as many times as you like — your scores and feedback are saved per interviewer in the Reviews tab, so you can watch yourself improve.
faq.q5Q: Is this like a real interview?
faq.q5A: Close. It's a live voice conversation that reacts to your answers, grounded in your CV and the specific job, with interviewers that stay in their lane — HR, hiring manager, or specialist. The main difference is it scores content only, where a real interview also weighs delivery.

chat.kindOpenerBuild: Welcome — I’m ARIA. We’ll build a CV that helps you apply with purpose, not blindly. Message me anytime as we create it, and come back to edit or refine it whenever you need — here’s how we’ll begin.
chat.kindOpenerTailor: New tailoring. Paste the job you're going for and I'll read it properly.
chat.pickModeBuild: Let's build it together. Here's how it'll run.
chat.pickModeTailor: Good — paste the job below and I'll read it properly.
chat.captureJobWithBrief: Here's how I read it — check I've got this right before I touch your CV.
chat.captureJobNoBrief: I couldn't fully read that one, but I've got the job saved. Have a look and carry on.
chat.tailorStartDone: Your tailored copy is saved — your original is untouched. Now let me read it against the job properly and show you what to change.
chat.tailorStartFailed: I couldn't set up the tailored copy just now — pick a CV again and I'll retry.
chat.confirmBriefWithSource: Good. I'll tailor a copy of {{title}} — one moment.
chat.confirmBriefNoSource: Good. Which CV should I work from?
chat.scanDone: Here's where you stand. The red and amber sections are where the work is.
chat.buildScanGapNudge: You're at {{fit}}% fit for this job. The biggest gaps are in {{sections}} — this role wants {{keywords}}, which I don't see on your CV yet. If any of that is truthfully yours, open the Live preview and add it to those sections.
chat.buildScanStrong: Nice — you're already a {{fit}}% fit for this job. Have a look at any amber sections if you want to push it higher, or you're good to finish.
chat.scanInsufficientCredits: You need {{required}} credits for a full scan and you have {{current}}. Top up and I'll run it.
chat.scanFailed: I couldn't finish the scan just now — try again in a moment.
chat.fixPickWithKeywords: {{section}}: this job leans on {{keywords}} — which one should we sharpen?
chat.fixSkills: Here's what the job asks for that your CV doesn't claim yet.
chat.fixSkillsIntro: Let's get your skills right for this job — I can suggest ones grounded in your CV, or you add your own. You choose what actually fits.
chat.fixGuide: {{section}}: this one's about completeness, not wording — here's what's missing and where to add it.
chat.projectIdeaOpener: Let's build "{{title}}". To start — what does it do, or what problem does it solve?
chat.projectIdeasNone: Nothing came to mind from your CV just yet — let's shape a project together.
chat.sectionDismissed: Noted — I'll leave {{section}} out of your score. You can put it back any time.
chat.fixSummary: I'll rewrite your summary around this job. First — where are you in your career?
chat.pickEntryWithGaps: Right — {{title}}. The job leans on {{gaps}}. Did you do either of those here? Tell me what you actually did.
chat.pickEntryNoGaps: Right — {{title}}. Tell me one thing you actually did there.
chat.fixMovedScore: {{section}} moved {{from}} → {{to}}{{bandNote}} Re-scoring is free, so keep going.
chat.fixSavedNoMove: {{section}} is saved. The score didn't move much yet — it usually takes a couple of entries.
chat.beginBuild: Before we begin, I need one quick bit of context about your experience.
chat.beginBuildUpload: Good — before you send me the file, two quick questions so I read it properly. First, where are you in your career?

upload.prompt: Send me the CV you already have and I'll read it into this session.
upload.verbatimNote: I'll bring it in exactly as you wrote it — nothing rewritten. We'll improve it together from there.
upload.typedInstead: No problem — we'll do it the usual way. Let's start with your contact details.
upload.failed: Something went wrong reading that CV. Nothing was charged — try again, or type it out instead.
upload.doneComplete: That's a complete CV. I've opened the editor on the right — every line is yours to change, and I'm here whenever you want a section sharpened.
upload.doneIncomplete: Got it. It's missing {{missing}}, so the editor stays locked until we fill those in — let's do that together now, starting with your contact details.
